list.listitem: Consider primary antibody deficiency (PAD) in patients with recurrent, severe, unusual, or persistent infections, especially upper and lower respiratory infections. C
The diagnostic approach involves measuring serum IgG, IgA, IgM levels; responses to pneumococcal and tetanus vaccines; and optionally quantitation of B cells in the blood. C
Patients who cannot make protective antibodies are eligible for immunoglobulin-replacement therapy and should be referred to an immunologist for further evaluation and treatment. C
Immunoglobulin-replacement therapy is indicated for all patients with IgG levels <200 mg/dL and selectively for persons with IG levels of 200 mg/dL or higher. A

Prognosis depends on the specific diagnosis, age at onset and diagnostic delay, extent of organ damage at presentation, and presence of other immune dysregulation, e.g., autoimmune disease. However, most patients will have an average life span. B

background.definition: Primary antibody deficiencies are a heterogeneous group of immune deficiencies with absence or marked reduction of one (e.g., selective IgA) or more classes (e.g., Bruton’s agammaglobulinemia) of immunoglobulins, and/or the inability to provide antibody-mediated protection against pathogens. They result from abnormalities of B-cell development or differentiation, or from defects in other cell lines (e.g., T cells) that affect B-cell function. Over 30 different predominantly antibody-deficient primary immune deficiencies are recognized. Conditions are defined by clinical manifestations and specific diagnostic findings.

list.listitem: The prevalence of diagnosed primary immunodeficiencies (PID) in the US is estimated at 1 per 1,200 persons with almost half of cases being primary antibody deficiencies (PAD).

PAD accounted for 63.4% of primary immunodeficiencies diagnosed in the US in 2015 at the Jeffrey Modell Centers Global Network, which is dedicated to the diagnosing and caring of patients with PID. Globally, 53% of all PID cases were PAD.
The most common PAD reported were selective IgA deficiency, common variable immunodeficiency, unspecified hypogammaglobulinemia, and specific antibody deficiency (normal IgG and B cells).
Inherited deficiencies in signaling molecules or enzymes in B-cell development, activation, and differentiation. Defects may be intrinsic to B cells or affect other cell lines.

The absence of antibodies inhibits microbial removal by opsonization and phagocytosis, complement activation, and pathogen and toxin neutralization. Patients have increased susceptibility to common and opportunistic infections of respiratory and gastrointestinal systems, caused by encapsulated extracellular bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumococcus, M. catarrhalis), but also viruses (enteroviruses) and parasites (G. lamblia).

A new neonatal screening test, the kappa-recombining excision circles, can identify newborns with severe B-cell deficiencies such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia, and is in use in some countries (e.g., Sweden, Spain, and Israel). C

Vaccination recommendations depend on the type of underlying antibody deficiency. Specific recommendations are available from the 2013 IDSA clinical practice guidelines for vaccination of the immunocompromised host. B
Live vaccines are contraindicated in patients with common variable immune deficiency (CVID) and agammaglobulinemia. It is safe to administer subunit and inactivated vaccines. B
Following a definite PAD diagnosis, consider referral for genetic counseling, especially if a molecular diagnosis is determined. This may assist with in utero diagnosis in future pregnancies. C
Diagnostic evaluation requires detailed clinical history, physical examination, family history, and laboratory tests. C

If PAD is suspected, initial diagnostic testing should include a CBC, quantitative measurement of serum immunoglobulins G, A, M (+/-E); serological responses to protein and polysaccharide vaccine antigens (DT, tetanus toxoid, H. influenzae, pneumococcus); and quantitative B cell, T cell, and NK immunophenotyping using flow cytometry. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Normal frequency of infection; daycare (children) passive smoking
Bronchial hyperreactivity, allergy, asthma, adenoidal hypertrophy
Inhaled foreign object, congenital anomaly, ciliary dyskinesia

list.listitem:
The more severe the antibody deficiency, the earlier the onset of symptoms. Four broad categories of B-cell deficiencies have been described:
Severe reduction in all serum immunoglobulin classes with profoundly decreased or absent B cells, e.g., Bruton’s agammaglobulinemia. Severe reduction in at least two serum immunoglobulin classes with normal low numbers of B cells, e.g., common variable immunodeficiency. Severe reduction in IgG and IgA with normal/elevated IgM and normal numbers of B cells. Immunoglobulin class or subclass deficiency with normal numbers of B cells, e.g., transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy.
Consider primary antibody deficiency (PAD) in patients with severe, persistent, unusual, and recurrent infection, especially of upper and lower airways.
The key word is unusual - an unusual organism, an unusual duration, an unusual complication, or an unusual severity of a “usual” infection should prompt suspicion of an immunodeficiency.

There are eight patterns of clinical presentations of PID, shown below:
Recurrent ear, nose, throat, and airway infections (including bronchiectasis), most commonly associated with primary antibody deficiency. Failure to thrive from early infancy, including intractable diarrhea, severe eczema. Recurrent pyogenic infection, including granulomatous inflammation and poor wound healing. Unusual infections or unusually severe course of infections. Recurrent infections with the same type of pathogen. Autoimmune or chronic inflammatory disease; lymphoproliferation. Characteristic combinations of clinical features in eponymous syndromes. Angioedema without urticaria.

Physician-diagnosed primary immunodeficiency in a family member is a significant risk factor for primary antibody deficiency in patients with recurrent infections, so a thorough family history should be sought in the patient’s history.

Autoimmune, lymphoproliferative, and granulomatous disease can accompany increased susceptibility to infection in some patients.
gives specific clinical manifestations of some main types of primary antibody deficiencies.
Family history of primary immunodeficiency or primary antibody deficiency is associated with an 8-fold increase in risk (95% CI 3-22).

If primary antibody deficiency is suspected, initial testing should include the following: Complete blood count with differential. Quantitative serum immunoglobulin G, A, M, (+/- E) concentrations. If initial responses were low or absent, measurement of specific antibodies to prior vaccines and response to booster vaccination. Lymphocyte subset analysis with flow cytometry measurement of B and T cell populations. B-cell enumeration and phenotyping.
Measurement of serum immunoglobulins may show reduced levels of one or more immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM) and should prompt referral to an immunologist.
See algorithm for a recommended approach to patients with suspected primary antibody deficiency ().
Patients with suspected or proven PAD should have an evaluation and follow-up by an experienced immunologist.
Patients and their carers should be educated about PAD to facilitate optimal outcomes.
Treatment should be individualized depending on the diagnosis and patient’s symptoms. C
Immunoglobulin replacement therapy is indicated for all patients with IgG levels <200 mg/dL and selectively for persons with IG levels of 200 mg/dL or higher. A
Immunoglobulin therapy can be administered intravenously or subcutaneously. A

Replacement immunoglobulin G (IV or SC) provides the first line of therapy for symptomatic patients with evidence of significant deficiency of antibody production. Its efficacy is well documented for X-linked agammaglobulinemia and CVID. It is also used in other less severe forms of primary antibody deficiency where there is evidence of specific antibody deficiency and given to IgA deficiency patients with low IgG.

Immunoglobulin therapy provides the antibody repertoire of thousands of healthy donors who have been rigorously screened. The dosage is determined by IgG trough levels and optimization of clinical response. Trough levels, blood cell counts, and serum chemistry (liver function tests, urea, creatinine) should be regularly monitored.

Immunoglobulin replacement therapy is indicated for all patients with IgG levels <200 mg/dL; for persons with IgG levels between 200 mg/dL and 500 mg/dL if there are frequent infections and defective antibody response to vaccine or common pathogens; and for patients with IgG >500 mg/dL if severe recurrent infections and evidence of specific antibody deficiency.

Immunoglobulin therapy can be administered intravenously (IVIg) or subcutaneously (SCIg), providing individualization of treatment. IVIg is administered every 2 to 4 weeks, and SCIg is given every 1 to 2 weeks. Monthly doses range from 400 mg/kg to 800 mg/kg
Replacement immunoglobulin therapy for most patients with the inability to produce protective antibodies to common pathogens is usually for life.
Long-term antibiotics may be required in addition to immunoglobulin replacement in PAD patients who continue to have bacterial infections.
Evaluation and follow-up by an experienced immunologist are strongly advised.

Prognosis depends on the specific type of primary antibody deficiency, age of onset of symptoms, delay in diagnosis, the extent of organ damage (e.g., bronchiectasis) by the time the patient presents, and presence of other immune dysregulation such as autoimmune disease. B

Despite increased morbidity, most patients will have an average lifespan. In a study of 179 patients with primary antibody deficiency in Australia, survival following diagnosis was reduced in patients with immune dysregulation, with a 75% survival at 20 years after diagnosis compared with 98% for those with infection-only phenotype. B

Lung imaging and function should be monitored periodically in PAD patients with increased risk for recurrent severe respiratory infections. High-resolution CT is used to screen for underlying bronchiectasis and other lung pathologies associated with PID. C

feature.caption: Clinical Factors That May Represent Primary Immunodeficiency.

tr.td: 1. 4 or more new ear infections within 1 year
2. 2 or more serious sinus infections within 1 year
3. 2 or more months on antibiotics with little effect
4. 2 or more episodes of pneumonia within 1 year
5. Failure of an infant to gain weight or grow normally
6. Recurrent deep skin or organ abscesses
7. Persistent thrush in mouth or fungal infection on skin
8. Need IV antibiotics to clear infections
9. 2 or more deep-seated infections, including septicemia

feature.caption: Distinguishing Features of Primary Antibody Deficiencies.

tr.td: Absent or small tonsils and lymph nodes; enteroviral meningoencephalitis
Generalized lymphadenopathy; splenomegaly; autoimmunity, e.g., inflammatory arthritis, enteropathy, cytopenia; granulomatous disease
Failure to thrive in children; clubbing and abnormal breath sounds associated with bronchiectasis, pneumonia, and lung fibrosis (XLA, CVID); malignancy in solid organ or lymphoma
